doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

title: Records at home and the decision to become a musician
summary: Music filled his family's homes, from Charlie Parker 78s to Garner, Vaughan and Roach, and his father let him be. In his senior year he vowed to become a musician. His uncle then called him for a gig at 17.

people.name: maternal grandfather of Michael Max Fleming

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Okay. See now you’re getting into some juicy stuff.

My mother played piano. Her father played piano. But my father played, and my aunts played, we call it the Victrola, the record player. So I had — my father made sure I heard every kind of music that ever existed.

So in other words, three years before that my aunt gave me, my aunt who was a sister to this brother, gave me a “Charlie Parker with Strings” 78 for my birthday. And all of my mother’s sisters were married to amateur musicians. One was a drummer, one was a piano player. So each time when I’d go to everybody’s house, and I was an only child, music was my babysitter. So at one place I’d hear Erroll Garner, you know. At another place I’d hear Sarah Vaughan. Each house, another house I’d hear Max Roach. So I was inundated with music between my father, who probably felt somehow I might one day be a musician although he didn’t want me to be. But he was very fatherly and he wasn’t going to destroy me. But I think he wanted me to be something else but he couldn’t deny that it was in me. And going back to your question, my senior year of high school I spent all that time saying, “Do you want to be a musician? If you want to be a musician are you aware, are you willing to pay the price to do all it takes to become a musician?” Going through stories of hardships that musicians went through and this and that. So halfway through, “YES!” I’m going to be a musician. And I say this now half-heartedly. But to me at that time that was — what do priests and nuns take? — a vow of poverty? So I was looking at it like that.

That’s a pretty mature attitude to even sort of be aware that it’s an important decision and that you’re going to have to pay some serious dues to do it. Maybe because you had musicians around you and your uncle and you were a little more aware of the realities of
